items.stimulus: An astronomy student models light from a distant star as two parallel rays, line $\ell$ and line $m$. The edge of a telescope mirror lies along line $t$, which crosses line $\ell$ at point $P$ and line $m$ at point $Q$. At point $P$, the angle between line $t$ (going from $P$ toward $Q$) and line $\ell$ (going to the right of $P$) measures $58^\circ$. At point $Q$, the angle between line $t$ (going beyond $Q$, away from $P$) and line $m$ (going to the left of $Q$) measures $x^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
items.stem: What is the value of $x$?
items.explanation: Line $t$ cuts parallel lines, so the corresponding angle at $Q$, between line $t$ going beyond $Q$ and line $m$ going to the right, is also $58^\circ$. Angle $x$ sits on the other side of line $m$ and forms a linear pair with that angle, so $x = 180 - 58 = 122$.

A.why: You treated lines $t$ and $m$ as perpendicular and took $90 - 58$. The question never says there is a right angle.

B.why: You found the corresponding angle at $Q$ and stopped there. Angle $x$ is the angle next to it on the straight line, so you still have to subtract it from $180$.

D.why: You added $90$ and $58$, as though $x$ were made of a right angle plus the given angle. Nothing in the figure supports that sum.
